Never, on any timescale that matters. The premise is a myth: at room temperature glass behaves as a solid, and its viscosity is so high that published estimates put noticeable flow beyond the age of the universe. Edgar Zanotto's 1998 calculation for cathedral glass gave roughly 10^32 years; his later 2017 work with Gupta revised it downward, but the result was still far past any practical span.

Old church panes are uneven because of how they were made. The crown and cylinder processes produced sheets of varying thickness, and glaziers often set the heavy edge at the bottom for stability. Not always, though: some old panes are thicker at the top or sides, which flow cannot explain. Roman glass and centuries-old telescope lenses also show no measurable sag.

Your windows will fail from seals, frames, or breakage long before the glass moves.
